source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Patching an answer with the model's own critique, with no outside signal, does not help and often hurts. This is the LLM version of a protective belt that only absorbs anomalies.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 before, 38.1 after round 1, 41.8 after round 2. GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. Max two rounds.
quote: If the LLM possesses the ability to self-correct, why doesn't it simply offer the correct answer in its initial attempt?
limits: Prompts taken from earlier papers; HotpotQA test set only 100 questions.
agent_relevance: G1/G2 confirmed: a patch round without a located failing output is a degenerating move and should be refused. Count patch rounds that add no new test pass.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (oracle condition)
finding: The same patch loop looks strong only when the true label tells it when to stop. The gain comes from the stopping signal, not from the patching.
numbers: With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49 to 59, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5. Without oracle all fall or stay flat.
limits: Oracle is unrealistic; the paper says it hides correct-to-wrong flips.
agent_relevance: S5 REVISE pays only if code supplies a signal that says whether a patch worked. Without it, stop after one round.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: When the model self-corrects it more often turns right answers into wrong ones than the reverse. Models cannot judge their own reasoning, so the loop cannot tell progress from degeneration.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time. On CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 flip many correct answers to wrong; GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo flip less.
limits: Only two rounds; confidence of stronger models lowers flips.
agent_relevance: A progress test must be computed by code (new facts predicted and confirmed), not asked of the model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (compute-matched)
finding: Multi-agent debate and self-consistency compared at equal response counts: voting wins, so more patching rounds lose to more independent samples.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2. Debate at 6 responses 83.2, at 9 responses 83.0.
limits: One model family, one dataset.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 and resampling instead of patching once a programme stalls.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?
finding: Critical survey of the self-correction literature. Reported wins mostly use oracle information or weak first-pass prompts.
numbers: Conclusions: no major work shows successful self-correction from self-prompted feedback in general tasks under fair settings; it works with reliable external feedback (code interpreters, tools) and after large-scale fine-tuning.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey, not new experiments; tasks with decomposable answers (for example CoVe) do allow intrinsic correction.
agent_relevance: Patch loops are justified only where outside feedback exists (tests, executors). Otherwise treat further patching as degenerating by default.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?
finding: The bottleneck is generating the feedback, not applying it. This matches Lakatos: the hard part is diagnosing which anomaly is real and where it sits.
numbers: Reflexion and RCI are cited as using oracle or external signals, flagged as unfair over-evaluation.
limits: Interpretation by the survey authors.
agent_relevance: Put effort into locating failures in code (G2), not into longer self-critique.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? (checklist)
finding: Splits research questions into intrinsic self-correction, external feedback and fine-tuning, and gives a checklist: equal compute, no oracle, strong first prompt.
numbers: Table 4 lists studies that used oracle information or weak initial prompts.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Use as the test protocol for any ablation of S5/S6 in our harness.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair of code is a protective-belt move with a price. When repair cost is counted, gains are modest, uneven, sometimes absent, and often below plain resampling at the same budget.
numbers: Metric pass@t (tokens). Success of repair, GPT-4's own feedback vs human feedback: overall 33.30% vs 52.60% (introductory 42.64 vs 62.21, interview 19.33 vs 45.67, competition 3.67 vs 14.67). 16 participants wrote 2 pieces of feedback for each of 40 failing programs.
quote: self-repair is not always the best strategy when compared to a non-repair baseline with the same sample budget
limits: HumanEval and APPS only; 40 programs in the human study; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G7: a patch round must beat a fresh sample at equal tokens or count as degenerating.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (stronger feedback model)
finding: Swapping in a stronger model only for the feedback step lifts weaker models above both baseline and self-repair. The repair stage is bottlenecked by diagnosis.
numbers: On APPS Code Llama and GPT-3.5 beat baseline and self-repair with GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 feedback; HumanEval gain grows with feedback strength. Self-repair gains over baseline: GPT-3.5 up to 3%, Code Llama up to 10%.
limits: The feedback model is still an LLM, so not a clean external signal.
agent_relevance: A separate checker can tell a real anomaly from noise; a same-model critic cannot.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (pass@t metric)
finding: They define pass@t, which charges tokens for sampling, feedback and repair, and compare to a no-repair baseline at equal budget. A ratio at or below 1 means the patching was degenerating.
numbers: Ratio against the same sample budget; stronger models see repair success and resampling success rise together.
limits: Per-task, two benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A ready recipe for a code-computed check of whether patching pays (G7).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion is a working agent loop with a Lakatos-like step: failure is turned into a stored lesson, and there is an explicit stop rule. It helps where a clean reward exists.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 80 to 91; MBPP Python 80 to 77 (worse); HumanEval Rust 60 to 68; ALFWorld +22 points in 12 trials over 134 tasks; HotPotQA +20 on 100 questions. ReAct-only agent stuck at 22% hallucination with no recovery.
limits: Needs a binary or scalar signal from the environment or tests.
agent_relevance: Retries on HotPotQA stopped after 3 consecutive failures: a ready-made degeneration stop. MBPP shows a noisy signal makes patching degenerate.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion (test reliability)
finding: Whether patching helps tracks the reliability of the test signal, measured by true-positive and false-positive rates of self-written unit tests.
numbers: HumanEval Python: TP 0.99, FN 0.40, FP 0.01, TN 0.60, base 0.80, Reflexion 0.91. MBPP Python: TP 0.84, FN 0.59, FP 0.16, TN 0.41, base 0.80, Reflexion 0.77.
limits: Tests produced by the model with chain-of-thought, at most 6 per task.
agent_relevance: A pass on model-written tests is weak evidence; G3 held-out checks matter. Do not count it as empirical progress.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion (memory cap)
finding: Memory is kept small: 1 experience on code, 3 on ALFWorld and reasoning. This caps how large the protective belt grows.
numbers: Memory limit 1 for programming, 3 for decision making and reasoning.
limits: Chosen for context length, not tested as a degeneration control.
agent_relevance: Keep carried lessons few and short.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: Underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Opposite failure to endless patching: reasoning models abandon a promising line too early. Wrong answers use more thought switches and more tokens.
numbers: On average 225% more tokens in incorrect than correct responses. A thought-switch penalty (alpha 3, beta 600) lifted QwQ-32B-Preview AIME2024 pass@1 38.3 to 44.1, GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1, MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7; R1-Distill-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8.
quote: models frequently switch between different reasoning thoughts without sufficiently exploring promising paths
limits: Decoding change on open models; strong penalty (alpha 20) with long duration lowered accuracy.
agent_relevance: This is the naive-falsification error: dropping a programme at the first anomaly. A detector needs a patch counter and a switch counter; Lakatos says give a young programme time.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: Underthinking of o1-like LLMs (prompt fix)
finding: Telling the model by prompt to stay on one thought did not help; only the decoding penalty did.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 AIME2024 pass@1 73.8 plain, 72.4 with prompt, 74.8 with TIP. QwQ UT score AIME 40.6 to 35.8 with TIP.
limits: Single test set per model.
agent_relevance: Enforce persistence or switching in code, not by instruction.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models (HypoGeniC)
finding: A working LLM system with programme-style logic: keep a bank of rival hypotheses, score each on new data, and replace failing ones with new ones built from the misfit examples.
numbers: Gain over few-shot: +31.7 (Shoe Sales), +13.9 (Deceptive Reviews), +3.3 (Headline), +24.9 (Tweet). Update stage added on average 0.7, 5.8, 8.1, 7.0 points over no-update. Claude-2.1 Deceptive Reviews 70.3 without update, 75.3 with.
limits: Classification with labels; replacement is by reward on known data, with no test that new hypotheses predict novel facts.
agent_relevance: Template for S6: rival hypotheses with running reward and a retire rule. Reward is a code-side progress measure, only on fit to known data.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models (HypoGeniC) (context limit)
finding: When training examples exceed the context window the no-update version degrades, while the update version stays stable.
numbers: Figures 4 and 5 show the no-update method falling as examples grow beyond the window.
limits: GPT-3.5-turbo window.
agent_relevance: A retained bank updated in chunks beats one long prompt in long loops.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Stating abstract hypotheses, then coding each and running it on examples, gives a two-layer programme: core idea plus testable belt. It beats direct prompting.
numbers: ARC, 100 random tasks, GPT-4: direct 17%, program only 23%, with generated hypotheses 30% (LLM summary filter), 33% with human selection. Chain-of-thought without programs: 19%.
limits: Fitting shown examples is not proof (G3). Memorisation checked and judged not to explain the gain.
agent_relevance: The checkable program is the belt; a held-out example is the novel-fact test.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2
finding: Agentic tree search for research with a hard cap on debugging depth. One of three fully AI-written papers passed workshop review; its content was a negative result.
numbers: 3 manuscripts among 43 workshop submissions; one scored 6.33 (6, 6, 7), two rejected. Maximum debug depth 3, debug probability 1.0, 21 nodes per stage, 1 hour per node.
limits: Workshop acceptance 60-80% versus 20-30% at main tracks; authors judge none at main-conference quality.
agent_relevance: Concrete budget numbers for a patch cap (depth 3).

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent test of AI Scientist v1. Its code edits shrink each iteration, a measurable sign of patching with diminishing returns.
numbers: Template 6,260 characters. Aider added 529 (+8%) in iteration 1, then 118, 83, 66, 21. 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed to run; 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had hallucinated numbers; median 5 citations.
limits: Small sample (7 manuscripts, 12 ideas); one system.
agent_relevance: Shrinking edit size is a cheap, code-computable stagnation signal for S6, though only a proxy.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist (novelty)
finding: Novelty checks by keyword search judged known ideas as new, so a model's novelty claim is not a valid progress test.
numbers: Ideas such as micro-batching for SGD were flagged as novel. Cost $6 to $15 per paper with 3.5 human hours.
limits: Same small sample.
agent_relevance: Supports G8: progress is judged by running or retrieval, not by the model.

source: Branahl (2024) Stagnant Lakatosian Research Programmes
finding: Adds a third label to progressive and degenerating: stagnant, meaning no empirical progress for benign outside reasons. Four criteria must all hold.
numbers: Criteria: pure theorizing for too long; no rival progressing; benign external limits; still valuable. Example numbers: accelerators reach about 10^4 GeV vs GUT scale 10^15 GeV; Park, Leahey and Funk: disruptiveness fell 90% across 45 million papers over six decades.
limits: Philosophy paper on physics, no AI test; author calls claims speculative; no fixed time limit.
agent_relevance: Gives a third verdict for the impasse detector: a stall from a missing tool (no executor, no data) is not degeneration. Ask for the tool instead of patching.

source: Denario project (2025) Deep knowledge AI agents for scientific discovery
finding: Section 7.4 applies Lakatos, Kuhn and Feyerabend to LLM science. It asks whether training data is a new hard core and whether a programme without a human-readable core can be progressive.
numbers: Text only, no measurement. Pipeline caps: n_reviews usually 1, 3 to 8 plan steps, n_rounds 500, stop when code failures exceed n_fails, idea maker/hater 3 iterations.
quote: LLMs may challenge existing research programmes
limits: I read the HTML in two chunks through a summarising fetch; the Lakatos passage is brief.
agent_relevance: Existing agent loops already use hard caps as crude degeneration stops. More plan-review rounds made plans overly complex, which supports a cap of 1.

source: Denario project (2025) Deep knowledge AI agents for scientific discovery (performative rationality)
finding: Warns that scientific rationality may become performative, with coherence and citation density standing in for theory depth or experimental validation.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Opinion in a system paper.
agent_relevance: Matches G10: fluent, coherent text is not evidence of progress.

source: Search gap: direct Lakatos tests on LLMs (this run)
finding: I found no paper that measures LLMs against Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating test or tests hard-core protection in models. Search tools were rate limited or out of budget, so this is a coverage gap, not proof none exists.
numbers: One WebSearch worked; arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
limits: Coverage gap.
agent_relevance: The progressive-versus-degenerating signal for S6 is a design to build and test with our own harness, not a result to cite.
